title: AMP-CMD Opportunity Pool
bodyHtml:
OP Funded Proposal Abstracts

 
CYCLE 1
Four projects were awarded during cycle 1 of the opportunity pool.

 

1. A consortium-wide common tool box for transcript perturbation in multiple diabetes-relevant cell types

PIs: Anna Gloyn, Karen Mohlke

Abstract: A central goal of the AMP-CMD consortium is to deliver a robust set of genes or “effector transcripts” responsible for mediating T2D-GWAS associations. Perturbing candidate effectors is critical to provide evidence for causality. Many studies of function are limited to a single cell type and context, leading to incomplete or inaccurate conclusions about a gene’s contribution to disease mechanisms, especially genes with pleiotropic effects. Studies of transcript effects on multiple diabetes-related cell processes in multiple cell types/contexts will provide robust data to define risk genes and inform further studies of function. Aim 1: Prioritize genes for collaborative studies of knockdown effects on diabetes- relevant cell functions. We will collect genes identified in the initial AMP-CMD RFA, updated AMP-T2D analyses, and the Effector Transcript Working Group. Genes will be prioritized based on evidence for pleiotropy across diabetes-relevant cell types. In parallel we will generate a cell-type-specific pooled library focused on both genes and regulatory elements predicted to work through two major liver cell types.  This will serve as a paradigm for how the library can be scaled and expanded to serve additional investigators.  Aim 2: Generate lentiviral guideRNA libraries for CRISPR inhibition across cell types. We will clone gRNAs into plasmid vectors and generate lentivirus for ~180 gene promoters using 4 gRNAs/promoter in arrayed format and 10 gRNAs/promoter in pooled format. This cost-effective resource is scalable and future libraries could include gRNAs for enhancers.  For the NAFLD library we will clone 4K gRNAs targeted at both genes and enhancers. Libraries will be infected in AAVS1-integrated doxycycline-inducible dCas9-KRAB inducible cell lines, which allows to generate homogenous, targeted cell populations in a reversible, tunable and efficient manner. Future Aim 3: Determine the consequences of gene knockdown. Multiple groups will use these libraries in at least islet beta cells, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and myocytes and measure, depending on cell type, insulin secretion, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, lipid accumulation, mitochondrial function, and other assays.

 

2. Comprehensive functional characterization of metabolic disease-associated variants in relevant cell types

PIs: Michael Stitzel and Ryan Tewhey

Abstract: Our understanding of the genetics of Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and other common metabolic diseases (CMD) has contributed significantly towards a fundamental goal of identifying common and rare genetic markers (e.g., single nucleotide polymorphisms, rare variants, structural variation etc.) associated with complex phenotypic traits including risk of disease. Variant catalogues have rapidly expanded, propelled by larger genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and biobanks. However, two characteristics of most GWAS variants impede efforts to translate genetic associations into molecular and pathophysiologic effects: (i) they reside in non-coding regions of the genome and modulate gene expression; and (ii) linkage disequilibrium and lagging efforts to leverage recombination across world populations imposes constraints on our ability to localize individual causal allele(s) within large haplotype blocks. Comprehensive first-principle, molecular-level understanding of CMD-associated non-coding variant function is essential to identify candidate causal gene regulatory variants, define their allelic effects on transcriptional activity, and determine the cell type(s) and context(s) in which they act. To identify functional T2D variants with expression-modulating activity in human (pre)adipocytes, we will test a 60k oligo T2D Module (T2DM) MPRA library containing ~8,800 fine-mapped, high priority T2D variants from DIAMANTE, UK Biobank, and Biobank Japan as well as a panel of positive and negative control sequences. Preliminary T2DM MPRA analyses nominated 176 T2D variants as functional expression modulating variants (emVars) in one of five ENCODE cell types (K562, A549, GM12878, SK-N-SH, and HepG2) and/or human EndoC-ßH3 ß-cells. We will extend this T2DM MPRA library to identify T2D emVars in SGBS (pre)adipocytes. Importantly, we will share the list of emVars and provide the T2DM library to AMP-CMD investigators to enable discovery of T2D variant effects in additional cell types and contexts.  We will also contribute our expertise with MPRA to consortium efforts to create a new MPRA library representing new T2D/CMD signals, disease variants, and design parameters. We will test and validate cell- and context-specific effects of variants in this library using human EndoC-ßH3 ß-cells to identify and nominate functional emVars within these new association signals.

 

3. Stem cell models for interrogating T2D effector gene function and benchmarking T2D relevant phenotypes

PIs: Wenli Yang, Paul Titchenell, and Klaus Kaestner

Abstract: A major goal of the AMP-CMD consortium is the functional interrogation of T2D-associated genes in relevant cell types. Increasing evidence suggests that many of the predicted candidate genes have pleiotropic effects across multiple cell types and may even function during tissue development. Critical for the success of AMP-CMD is the establishment, validation, and sharing of models and metabolic assays of insulin action and of endocrine hormone production. To this end, a set of well characterized human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines that serve as a renewable resource for generating cellular models for assaying gene function is required.  Furthermore, PSC cell models of impaired insulin signaling, or defective pancreatic endocrine function are necessary as a ‘gold standard’ to validate any assay employed by AMP-CMD to evaluate candidate T2D genes.  Establishing these cell lines and models will be extremely valuable to the AMP-CMD consortium for benchmarking T2D relevant phenotypes for gene validation. Constitutive CRISPR-mediated gene manipulation in PSC lines is not suitable for studying gene function in differentiated cells if the gene product affects cell differentiation. The inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) gene perturbation systems are ideal alternatives that allow reversible and differentiation-stage specific gene suppression (“knockdown”) and activation, respectively. Aim 1: To generate and characterize inducible and reversible CRISPRi and CRISPRa human induced pluripotent human stem cell lines 1a.  We will target the CLYBL safe harbor locus of a well characterized line to generate dox-inducible CRISPRi and CRISPRa cell lines expressing dCas9-KRAB and dCas9-VPR, respectively.  1b.  We will extensively characterize the resulting lines for differentiation into hepatocytes, adipocytes, myocytes and pancreatic beta cells and tunability of the system.  Aim 2: To benchmark assays of insulin action and insulin secretion in hiPSC-derived cells using CRISPRi and CRISPRa perturbation of validated model target genes 1a.  We will suppress expression of AKT2 using CRISPRi and differentiate these cells into hepatocytes, myocytes and adipocytes and perform insulin action and metabolic physiological measurements in the AKT2 knockdown cells. 1b.  We will suppress and activate expression of GCK and differentiate these cells into beta cells and perform glucose stimulation of insulin secretion assays.

 

4. A consortium-wide modular MPRA resource to assess cellular contexts of T2D variants

PIs: Jacob Kitzman, Steve Parker, and Adelaide Tovar

Abstract: The AMP-CMD Genetics Working Group (GWG) recently released an updated trans-ancestry list of 667 T2D signals. Hence, there is urgent demand for a common resource to functionally comb through densely linked sets of candidate variants and define the cellular and environmental contexts of their regulatory activity. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) enable high-throughput regulatory element classification. Recent studies have employed MPRAs to test panels of putative regulatory sequences and to identify functional variants associated with a wide variety of traits [1–4], including in the context of T2D [5]. However, existing and ongoing T2D MPRAs were generated with outdated variant lists derived from 403 European signals reported by the DIAMANTE consortium in 2018 [6]. Thus, current MPRA libraries will miss an additional 264 T2D GWAS signals that have emerged in the past three years and all TOPMed-identified rare variants. To immediately address this urgent gap, we will create a modular, portable MPRA as a shared resource across AMPCMD to screen variants from the current T2D GWAS signals and TOPMed rare variants. Earlier T2D MPRA screens have focused on pancreatic beta cells; however, T2D etiology is complex and regions across several tissue types are enriched for heritability [7–11]. Additionally, genetic risk may be modified by environmental factors, meaning variant effects may only be detected after specific perturbations.  Existing MPRAs are ill-suited to capture these effects because they generally (1) use generic housekeeping gene promoters, which do not reflect cell-specific regulatory effects, and (2) are conducted under basal conditions. To address this gap, we will use our state-of-the-art MPRA system to represent all current variants at T2D loci in the context of multiple cell-type-specific promoters.  Aim 1: Construct an MPRA resource to classify regulatory activity at all known T2D-associated variants. We will use the ChromBPNet deep learning framework to optimally design oligos that span variants of interest, selected from the curated AMP-CMD GWG signal list and TOPMed rare variants. Then, we will clone these oligos into a multi-promoter MPRA vector. Using UM1-appropriated funds, we will screen human adipocytes, beta cells, hepatocytes, and myocytes to systematically assess enhancer activity for each element, in basal and stimulated states. We will make the library and screening results broadly available across AMPCMD, including data deposition in the Common Metabolic Diseases Genome Atlas (CMDGA) and Knowledge Portal (CMDKP). Aim 2: Design a comprehensive synthetic MPRA library to measure allelic effects at active T2Dassociated regions. We hypothesize that the primary mechanism through which T2D-associated common variants act is alteration of regulatory activity. Informed by the results of the activity screen in Aim 1, we will generate allelic versions of all oligos with enhancer activity. Additionally, we will target a subset of loci for (1) saturation mutagenesis and (2) driver nucleotide analysis, where densely tiled inserts spanning the nucleotide context of the variant(s) of interest will be synthesized. We will share broadly across AMP-CMD.

CYCLE 2
Two projects were funded for cycle 2 of the opportunity pool.

 

1. Generation of transcriptional and epigenomic annotations for hypothalamus, amygdala and hippocampus: utility for the identification of the neural cell-types and regulatory pathways important in human obesity

PIs: Ines Barroso, Timothy Frayling, Jonathan Mill

Abstract: Linking disease-associated genetic variants to epigenomic datasets from disease relevant tissues and cell types has been critical to nominate effector transcripts and begin to elucidate pathways related to disease. Previous studies have highlighted the critical role of gene regulation in various brain regions - in particular, the hypothalamus, cortex, amygdala and hippocampus - in pathways impacting human obesity/BMI. However, detailed genomic regulatory profiling across neural cells in these brain regions from human post-mortem samples is lacking. We are addressing this critical gap by generating data resources that will be of use to researchers in the obesity and metabolism field, and to researchers focused on brain disorders. 

Aim 1. Isolate single-nuclei from 3 brain regions (hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus) from 10 human donors and perform transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiling using the 10x genomics multiome approach for snRNA-seq/snATAC-seq.

Aim 2. Profile markers of genomic regulation in purified nuclei populations from 3 key neural cell-types (neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglial) isolated from the same 3 post-mortem brain regions (hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus) in the same 10 human donors. We will quantify 2 markers of gene regulation: DNA methylation and lysine H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac), providing more detailed information on the regulation of transcription in neural cell populations not obtainable from single-nuclei (Aim 1).

Aim 3. Prioritise brain regions/cell-types enriched for obesity/BMI heritability. We will employ a range of established and novel analytical methods for enrichment analysis and integrate these data with BMI associated genetic variation (from the GWAS of >4 million).

Aim 4. Generate lasting publicly available human brain genomic resources for the broader scientific community. In addition to the new datasets generated in Aims 1 and 2, we have equivalent annotations generated from prefrontal cortex from the same individuals which we will release together in a combined human brain dataset.

Our study is an important advance from genetic association to mechanism - refining BMI-associated signals identified in 4 million people and linking them to underlying biology. An improved knowledge of the brain’s involvement in obesity will identify novel pathways and help identify targets for anti-obesity drug development, a focus of the current AMP Common Metabolic Disease initiative.

 

2. Genomic profiling of acinar and ductal cells to annotate diabetes and glycemic trait loci in the exocrine pancreas

PI: Kyle Gaulton

Abstract: The exocrine pancreas is comprised of acinar and ductal cells which are responsible for the production and secretion of digestive enzymes into the gut. The exocrine pancreas regulates insulin secretion and beta cell function through multiple avenues including via the digestive system and incretin pathway as well as direct signaling to beta cells. Furthermore, the exocrine pancreas contributes to cystic fibrosis-related diabetes and potentially type 1 diabetes by promoting inflammation in the pancreas. Despite the biological relevance of exocrine cells to diabetes and glycemia, however, a comprehensive annotation of cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in exocrine cells, diabetes and glycemic trait loci that affect exocrine cell regulatory activity, genes linked to risk variant activity in exocrine cells, the cellular phenotypes of target genes in exocrine cells, and how these phenotypes may impact diabetes pathogenesis is currently lacking. Furthermore, recent studies have identified sub-types of exocrine cells such as REG+ acinar and MUC5b+ ductal cells, and the relative contribution of different exocrine sub-types to diabetes risk and glycemia are unknown. Our overall goal in this proposal is to annotate diabetes and glycemic trait variants and genes affecting the exocrine pancreas. Critically, this work is highly distinct from on-going work in AMP-T2D to profile beta cells and other endocrine cells as the genomic profiles of exocrine cells are distinct from endocrine cells, different risk loci affect exocrine and endocrine cell regulatory activity, and exocrine cells likely contribute to disease risk via distinct mechanisms. Furthermore, the genomic data we are generating from whole pancreas tissue enables effective annotation of the exocrine pancreas, as opposed to purified pancreatic islets where exocrine cells are preferentially excluded.

Aim 1: Identify diabetes and glycemic trait variants affecting exocrine cell cRE activity. In this Aim we will process and cluster single cell multiome data from 75+ whole pancreas samples from the nPOD repository and define acinar and ductal sub-types. We will define cREs in each cell type and sub-type and annotate fine-mapped variants overlapping cRE definitions. Next, we will perform chromatin QTL (caQTL) mapping and fine-mapping of acinar and ductal cREs and co-localize exocrine caQTLs with diabetes and glycemia association signals. Finally, we will perform massively-parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) using variant libraries generated by the consortium in acinar and ductal cell lines. The results of this Aim will provide fine-mapped variants at diabetes and glycemic trait loci that affect exocrine cell type and sub-type regulatory activity. 

Aim 2: Define target genes of exocrine cREs affected by diabetes and glycemic trait variant activity. In this Aim we will link cREs affected by fine-mapped variants to their putative target genes. We will first identify 3D chromatin interactions between cREs and gene promoter regions using HiChIP assays in FACS-sorted primary acinar and ductal cells. We will next generate activity-by-contact (ABC) links between cREs and gene promoters in acinar and ductal sub-types using single cell multiome from Aim 1. Finally, we will annotate target genes of cREs expressed in acinar and ductal sub-types using expression profiles from single cell multiome. The results of this Aim will provide target genes of exocrine cCREs affected by diabetes and glycemic variants. 

Aim 3: Characterize cellular phenotypes of target genes in acinar and ductal cells. In this Aim we will perform epigenomic silencing of ~3-4 cCREs affected by diabetes and glycemic variants and target gene(s) of these cCREs using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) in acinar or ductal cell lines. For each silenced cCRE and gene we will measure effects on gene expression using RNA-seq, apoptosis, ER stress, and secretion of digestive enzymes (for acinar cells) and bicarbonate (for ductal cells). The results of this Aim will provide cellular phenotypes of disease-relevant cCREs and genes linked to cCREs. This project is a collaboration between PI Gauton at UC San Deigo, who has expertise in diabetes genetics and single cell genomics, and co-Is Amundadottir and Arda at the NCI, who have expertise in exocrine pancreas disease and genomics, respectively. We will deposit raw data from single cell assays in 75 pancreas samples, MPRA assays in acinar and ductal cells, HiChIP in acinar and ductal cells and epigenome editing assays of ~3- 4 cCREs and target genes into the CMDGA, as well as all annotations derived from these data such as cCRE definitions, target gene links, caQTLs, variants affecting reporter activity, and cellular phenotypes.

CYCLE 3
Three projects were funded for cycle 3 of the opportunity pool.

 

1. Systematic functional characterization of consortia prioritized type-2 diabetes effector transcripts in vivo 

PI: Marcel den Hoed

In 2016, 1.6 million people died from diabetes, making it the 7th most common cause of death worldwide. Multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci that are robustly associated with type-2 diabetes (T2D) 1,2. However, for the vast majority of associated loci, candidate genes have not yet been functionally characterized. Currently ongoing efforts are typically cell-based, and – while informative – cannot model the complex interactions that occur between cell types, tissues and organs in a live, intact, vertebrate organism. Mouse models on the other hand lack the throughput to systematically characterize the role of many genes in T2D-related traits. In line with this, only a few handfuls of signals are currently explored using mouse models in AMP-CMD. Striving for an in vivo model system that supports a higher throughput, the den Hoed lab generated and validated a pipeline that uses CRISPR/Cas9 3, in vivo fluorescence imaging, and deep learning-based neural networks for image analysis to systematically characterize the role of candidate genes in T2D-related traits in live, intact zebrafish larvae. By phenotypically characterizing 59 human candidate genes for effects across multiple tissues in 6604 CRISPR-edited zebrafish larvae, we recently identified a role in T2D traits – i.e., beta cell mass, average and total beta cell ins expression, liver fat, and/or glucose content – for 23 candidate genes. Additional analyses (in collaboration with Flannick) show that these genes are enriched for common and rare variant associations with T2D risk in humans when compared with the 25 genes that do not show such effects when perturbed in zebrafish larvae. Recently, the Gloyn and den Hoed labs combined gene perturbation experiments in zebrafish larvae with human beta cell models (inc. EndoC-ßH1 and stem-cell derived islet-like cells) to study the T2D-risk gene RREB14, highlighting the benefit of functionally characterizing putative effector transcripts using complimentary model systems. Here, we aim to:Perturb and functionally characterize 40 putative effector transcripts for T2D risk in live, intact zebrafish larvae, focusing on genes identified through one of two tracks: 1. The NEWS team (Claussnitzer & Gloyn) have used a range of approaches to prioritize 200 putative effector transcripts for T2D which act through multiple diabetes relevant tissues. In a previously funded OP project, collaborators from the NEWS team are using a CRISPRi approach to investigate the role of these genes in four human cell types (beta cell, myocyte, adipocyte and hepatocyte) using diabetes relevant assays. Here, we propose to characterize the role of 25 of these transcripts that: i) are predicted to act through pancreatic beta cells, hepatocytes, and/or adipocytes; and ii) show either strong evidence, or no evidence of a role in T2D traits when perturbed in relevant human cell lines. In vivo confirmation of a role for effector transcripts showing strong evidence in vitro confirms the cell autonomous effect prevails in more complex environments; while an effect in vivo for effector transcripts that do not show an effect in vitro suggests such transcripts either act through (an)other cell type(s), or require more complex interactions than a cell line can model. 2. The Penn, Portal and TOPMed teams develop and use state of the art bioinformatics approaches to prioritize putative effector transcripts based on associations with T2D for variants of unknown significance in increasingly large whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing data sets. Since prediction of variant effects is based on a large number of assumptions and structural analogies, we suggest to functionally characterize 15 putative effector transcripts in vivo that may be nominated by the three teams (i.e., five per team) based on T2D associations with presumed functional variants.This may: a) yield in vivo evidence for a role of previously uncharacterized effector transcripts in T2D traits; and b) be a first step towards in vivo validation of in silico variant effect prediction approaches.

 

2. Method to Identify Transcription Factors Disrupted by GWAS Variants

PI: Hae Kyung Im

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and other genomic studies have found many variants that are statistically associated with common metabolic disease risk and related traits1–3. However, such studies do not identify specific causal variants nor do they determine the biological mechanisms underlying disease. To help identify effector genes, my team has developed genetic predictors of gene expression levels using data from the GTEx consortium4,5, which covers tissue across the human body. These predicted gene expression levels prioritize target genes for drug development and drugs for repurposing. However, many of the loci remain unexplained with current approaches. Given the growing consensus that these loci may alter the binding of transcription factors, we propose to extend the idea behind PrediXcan7 to transcription factor binding. That is, we want to generate genetic predictors of TF binding and correlate them with common metabolic disease (CMD) risk and related traits. However, generating the ChIP-seq data necessary to train individual-level predictors for thousands of TF/tissue pairs would require hundreds of thousands of experiments, which is not feasible. To date, only androgen receptor (AR) in prostate tissue has reported genetic predictors8. To overcome this hurdle, we generated compelling preliminary data showing that it is possible to train genetic predictors of TF binding using just a handful of experiments by leveraging the latest advances in deep learning approaches that predict epigenetic features directly from DNA sequences. We chose the current state of the art method, Enformer 9, which yields predicted epigenomes that are strikingly similar to observed values across the genome but have inconsistent performance across individuals. Specifically, while Enformer predictions of individual expression levels significantly correlate with observed data, the correlation is frequently (erroneously) negative leading many in the field to dismiss its utility10,11. The goal of this proposal is to develop TFXcan, a conceptually simple extension of PrediXcan that uses genetic predictors of TF binding to inform the mechanism of CMD GWAS loci. To accomplish this we will fine-tune Enformer to improve the personalized prediction and expose it to more disease relevant epigenomic data to improve prediction in contexts relevant to CMD pathogenesis. Using this foundation model, we will train predictors of TF binding relevant for CMD, and link them to GWAS loci. Aim 1 Improve Enformer personalized prediction and CMD relevant representation. For this purpose, we will fine-tune Enformer using personalized DNA sequences matched with RNA sequence data in GTEx, modifying the objective function to penalize the model when correlation across individuals is negative. We will also train Enformer using the Common Metabolic Diseases Genome Atlas (CMDGA) data so that the model parameters are better aligned with CMD relevant contexts. Large-scale computations of all aims will be performed on Argonne National Laboratory’s supercomputers. Aim 2: Augment Enformer to predict the binding for thousands of TF/tissue pairs. We will gather andformat the thousands of currently available ChIP-seq experiment data from Cistrome DB12. We will test different deep learning architectures, more traditional machine learning approaches, and different training schedules to optimize prediction of TF binding. Aim 3: Develop S-TFXcan a computationally feasible approach that infers the effect of TF binding regulation in CMD using GWAS summary statistics. To apply this approach to large GWAS studies, we will train traditional linear predictors of TF binding, i.e. linear combination of SNP data. Current suite of PrediXcan methods can be applied to these predictors allowing us to infer the correlation between genetically predicted TF binding and CMD and related traits using summary GWAS results. In summary, our project harnesses advances in AI to integrate data from the CMDGA, GTEx, and CistromeDB to inform the mechanisms that drive common metabolic diseases. Extensive preliminary results and the team’s experience with large-scale computing demonstrate feasibility. This proposal will generate software, prediction models, and mapping of TF to CMD, which will be shared broadly, maximizing the impact of our work.

 

2. Functional Interrogation in sympathetic neurons of genes associated with human obesity - and T2D

PI: Ana Domingos

Aims: Sympathetic neurons exert direct control over whole-body metabolism and energy dissipation by triggering lipolysis and thermogenesis within adipose tissues, and influencing glucose homeostasis via the pancreas, and the liver. The Domingos lab is currently investigating the release of various factors by sympathetic neurons, in addition to norepinephrine, which play a role in metabolic regulation. Some of these factors are genetically linked to human obesity. However, the functional roles of these genes in relation to human obesity and type-2 diabetes (T2D) are still largely unknown, as is their expression within sympathetic neurons. Our initial work on creating the first integrated single-cell atlas of cervical sympathetic neurons has revealed that several genes associated with human obesity and T2D are highly expressed within clusters of these neurons. Additionally, we have identified the molecular targets of anti-obesity and T2D drugs within these clusters. We propose a comprehensive pipeline for studying sympathetic neurons, which will aid in the early mechanistic assessment of genes associated with human obesity and T2D. First, we will sequence additional ganglia to construct SympAtlas, a comprehensive molecular atlas encompassing all sympathetic ganglia across anatomical levels. This data set will be integrated in the AMP-CMD's Knowledge Portal; and analyzed with manifold- and deep-learning algorithms. Second, we will use SympAtlas to investigate the expression of genes associated with obesity and T2D in specific subpopulations of sympathetic neurons.
